trial_name: VASST — Vasopressin versus Norepinephrine Infusion in Patients with Septic Shock (2008)
citation: Russell JA, Walley KR, Singer J, Gordon AC, Hebert PC, Cooper DJ, et al.; VASST Investigators. Vasopressin versus norepinephrine infusion in patients with septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(9):877-887
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, superiority
one_liner: Low-dose vasopressin did not significantly reduce 28-day all-cause mortality compared to norepinephrine in adult septic shock, though a potential survival benefit was observed in patients with less severe shock.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with septic shock enrolled within 24 hours of meeting eligibility criteria, requiring ongoing norepinephrine >=5 mcg/min (or equivalent) for at least 6 hours.
pico.intervention: Blinded vasopressin infusion titrated from 0.01 to 0.03 U/min delivered at a constant rate of 15 mL/hour, plus open-label vasopressors titrated to target MAP 65–75 mmHg.
pico.comparison: Blinded norepinephrine infusion titrated from 5 to 15 mcg/min delivered at an identical constant rate of 15 mL/hour, plus open-label vasopressors titrated to target MAP 65–75 mmHg.

background.existing_knowledge: Septic shock is characterized by vasoplegia and impaired vascular responsiveness, routinely managed with catecholamine vasopressors such as norepinephrine.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether adding low-dose non-catecholamine vasopressin to catecholamines improves survival or organ failure in established septic shock without causing prohibitive ischemic toxicity.
background.hypothesis: Low-dose vasopressin would reduce all-cause mortality compared with norepinephrine when added to background vasopressors in septic shock.

methods.design: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group controlled trial stratified by center and baseline shock severity.
methods.setting: 27 ICUs across Canada, Australia, and the USA; conducted 2001–2006.

inclusion: Adults with septic shock enrolled within 24 hours of eligibility
Ongoing vasopressor requirement with norepinephrine >=5 mcg/min (or equivalent) for >=6 hours (or fast-track option for higher vasopressor doses)
exclusion: NYHA Class III or IV heart failure
Vasopressin infusion during current admission prior to study
>24 hours elapsed since meeting eligibility criteria

methods.intervention: Blinded vasopressin infusion 0.01–0.03 U/min at 15 mL/hour constant rate; open-label vasopressors titrated to MAP 65–75 mmHg; open-label vasopressors weaned first.
methods.comparison: Blinded norepinephrine infusion 5–15 mcg/min at 15 mL/hour constant rate; open-label vasopressors titrated to MAP 65–75 mmHg; open-label vasopressors weaned first.
methods.blinding: Double-blind; central pharmacy prepared identical study infusions; clinicians, patients, and assessors remained blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: 776 patients required to detect 10% absolute mortality reduction (from expected 60% to 50%) with 80% power at alpha=0.05. Sample size increased to account for primary analysis restricted to randomized patients receiving infusion.
methods.primary_outcome: All-cause mortality at 28 days (primary cohort: randomized and infused).
secondary_outcomes: 28-day and 90-day mortality in pre-specified shock severity strata
Days alive and free of corticosteroid use

headline_bullets: Primary endpoint of 28-day mortality showed no significant difference between vasopressin and norepinephrine (35.4% vs 39.3%, P=0.26).
90-day mortality was lower with vasopressin in the pre-specified less severe shock stratum (35.8% vs 46.1%, RR 0.78, P=0.04).
Overall serious adverse event rates were identical between groups (10.3% vs 10.5%, P=1.00).
Norepinephrine infusion requirements were significantly lower in the vasopressin group during days 1–4 (P<0.001).

outcomes_table.note: Composite of prespecified serious adverse events

outcomes_table.outcome: Days alive and free of corticosteroids

subgroup_table.subgroup: Less severe shock: 28-day mortality (5–14 mcg/min NE at baseline)
Less severe shock: 90-day mortality (5–14 mcg/min NE at baseline)

safety: Serious adverse events occurred in 10.3% of vasopressin patients vs 10.5% of norepinephrine patients (P=1.00).
Digital ischemia occurred in 2.0% (8/396) with vasopressin vs 0.5% (2/382) with norepinephrine (P=0.11).
Hyponatremia occurred in 1.3% (5/396) with vasopressin vs 0.0% (0/382) with norepinephrine (P=0.06).

domains.notes: Central telephone randomisation using computer-generated sequence with variable block sizes; stratified by center and baseline shock severity.
Pharmacists prepared identical study infusions; clinicians, patients, and assessors were double-blinded.
802 randomised; 21 did not receive infusion, 2 withdrew consent, 1 lost to follow-up; primary cohort included 778 patients (396 vasopressin, 382 norepinephrine).
Study drug infusion rates differed by <2 mL/hour between groups; open-label vasopressin prohibited.

APACHE II scores similar (27.1 ± 7.6 vs 27.0 ± 7.1); minor baseline imbalances in age (61.8 ± 16.0 vs 59.3 ± 16.4) and coagulation dysfunction (22.0% vs 29.7%). Mean time to study drug was 11.5 ± 9.4 vs 11.9 ± 8.9 hours.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong given allocation concealment, double-blinding, and objective primary mortality assessment, with minor limitation in excluding 24 non-infused patients from primary cohort.

domains.notes: Adult ICU patients with septic shock requiring ongoing norepinephrine; excludes acute coronary syndromes, severe heart failure, mesenteric ischemia, and pregnancy.
High applicability to well-resourced ICUs utilizing norepinephrine as first-line therapy; less applicable to pediatric or non-ICU populations.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for adult ICU septic shock, but restricted in patients with severe arterial occlusive disease or cardiac compromise.

strengths: Rigorous capture of serious adverse events and organ dysfunction-free days
limitations: Primary cohort excluded 24 randomised patients who did not receive infusion
Vasopressin dose capped at 0.03 U/min (did not test higher rescue doses)
Enrolled between 2001–2006, prior to modern sepsis bundle updates

critical_appraisal.summary: VASST is a high-quality RCT demonstrating that low-dose vasopressin as an adjunct to norepinephrine does not reduce 28-day mortality overall, though subgroup analysis suggests potential benefit in less severe shock.
strengths: Standardized protocol for open-label vasopressor titration and weaning
weaknesses: Primary analysis restricted to randomized and infused cohort
Subgroup interaction test for shock severity was non-significant (P=0.10)

sections.authors_conclusion: Low-dose vasopressin did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with norepinephrine in patients with septic shock, though vasopressin may benefit patients with less severe shock.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Vasopressin should not replace norepinephrine as sole first-line therapy in septic shock, but serves as an effective second-line/adjunctive agent to spare catecholamines and increase MAP.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with septic shock requiring ongoing norepinephrine therapy.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Vasopressin should be routinely given to all septic shock patients as primary monotherapy.
implementation_caveats: Cap fixed low-dose vasopressin at 0.03 U/min
Monitor for digital and splanchnic ischemic complications
Monitor serum sodium for potential hyponatremia

controversies.topic: Subgroup interpretation in less severe shock
controversies.notes: Mortality benefit observed in the 5–14 mcg/min NE stratum (90-day RR 0.78, P=0.04), but interaction P-value was 0.10, prompting debate over potential false-positive subgroup finding.

A post-hoc analysis demonstrated significant interaction (P=0.008): vasopressin reduced 28-day mortality in steroid-treated patients (35.9% vs 44.7%, P=0.03) but not in non-steroid-treated patients (33.7% vs 21.3%, P=0.06).

context_related_trials.relation: Evaluated early vasopressin vs norepinephrine and hydrocortisone vs placebo in a 2x2 factorial trial; found no difference in kidney failure-free days.

unresolved_questions: Optimal timing and blood pressure threshold for initiating vasopressin relative to norepinephrine onset
Impact of combining early vasopressin with corticosteroids on long-term survival and renal replacement therapy

numbers_to_remember: Less severe shock 90-day mortality: 35.8% vs 46.1% (RR 0.78, P=0.04)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Norepinephrine remains the primary vasopressor in septic shock, with low-dose vasopressin added at 0.03 U/min to reduce catecholamine requirements or treat refractory vasoplegia.
